Red-winged Blackbird — Photographic Sequence

  1. Home
  3. Field notes

  5. Passeriformes
  6. Icteridae
  7. Red-winged Blackbird — Photographic Sequence

Agelaius phoeniceus

The Red-winged Blackbird photographs collected here span several encounters and changing conditions: a brief early spring snowfall, territorial calling from low branches, close-range views of the male’s epaulet and plumage, and females moving among grasses and cattails. For identification, habitat, and natural-history details, see the Agelaius phoeniceus species page.

Taken together, the photographs show two very different visual strategies within the same species. The male announces his presence through exposed perches, voice, posture, and color; the female is more easily absorbed into the vertical pattern and muted tones of the marsh.

First Spring Snow

The snowfall softened the wetland, muting the background and isolating the male among reeds and cattails. Against that subdued palette, even a partly visible epaulet becomes conspicuous.

E22A0287 gives the sequence its strongest environmental introduction. The bird remains relatively small within the frame, allowing the falling snow, cattails, and bending perch to carry as much of the atmosphere as the bird itself.


Red-winged Blackbird — First Spring Snow
A sentinel of the marsh, holding his ground as winter lingers.
Camera: Canon EOS 5D Mark IV
Lens: EF100-400mm f/4-5.6L IS USM
Settings: ISO 4000 • Aperture f/6.3 • Shutter 1/320 s
E22A0287 • Size: 2700 x 1800

Territorial Call

Plumage at Close Range

At close range, the male’s black plumage is no longer a single dark surface. Individual feather layers, subtle sheen, the folded wing, and the structure of the epaulet become visible.


Shoulder and Wing Detail

Settings: ISO 800 • Aperture f/6.3 • Shutter 1/1000 s
E22A0535 • Size: 3337 x 2225

E22A0531 returns from structure to behavior. It is not as strong a display photograph as E22A0784, but the close working distance gives the call a different immediacy.

Female Red-winged Blackbird

The female photographs change both the palette and the visual language of the page. Where the male is defined by glossy black plumage and conspicuous shoulder color, the female’s streaked brown pattern echoes grasses, seed heads, and cattails.

Lens: EF70-200mm f/2.8L IS II USM 2x

Photographer’s Perspective

The Red-winged Blackbird collection changed as closer encounters accumulated. The snowfall sequence first established the bird within the marsh and gave the page its strongest sense of weather and habitat. Later photographs moved progressively closer: territorial calling, a fully raised epaulet, direct eye contact, and feather structure. The female photographs then broadened the collection again, returning attention to the reeds and grasses while showing a very different plumage pattern and a quieter form of presence.

The photographs now form a progression:

weather and habitat → territorial display → direct awareness → plumage detail → female voice and concealment

That progression is why the Gallery can remain selective. The strongest photographs can carry the portfolio there, while this Photographic Sequence preserves the smaller changes in posture, behavior, and setting that connect the individual frames.
